label: Partition
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{Partition}
Let $\Gamma$ be a graph and $C$ be a subset of the vertices of $\Gamma$. If $C$ is a  perfect code of $\Gamma$, then the $|C|+1$ sets $\{\Gamma(c)~|~ c\in C\}$ and $C$ constitute a partition  of $V(\Gamma)$.
head: environment

label: LeftTrans-Lem
title: Lemma
body_md:
\cite{Weiyue-2026}\label{LeftTrans-Lem}
Let $\Gamma=\mathrm{BC}(G;R, L, S)$ be a bi-Cayley graph and $H$ and $K$ be  subgroups of $G$. Then, $H_0\cup K_1$ is a subgroup perfect code of $G$ if and only if $R\cup \{1_G\}$ is a left transversal of $H$ in $G\setminus S^{-1}*K$ and $L\cup \{1_G\}$ is a left transversal of $K$ in $G\setminus S*H$.
head: environment

label: LeftTransversal
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{LeftTransversal}
    Let $\Gamma=\mathrm{BC}(G;R, L, S)$ be a bi-Cayley graph and $H$ be a subgroup of $G$. Then, $H$ is a subgroup perfect code of $G$ if and only if both $R\cup S^{-1} \cup \{1_G\}$ and $L\cup S \cup \{1_G\}$ are left transversals of $H$ in $G$.
head: environment

label: SInterKH
title: Claim
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Suppose, to the contrary, that there exists an element $s\in S\cap KH$, then $s=kh$ for some $k\in K $ and $h\in H$. Hence, $sh^{-1}=k$ which implies that $(h^{-1})_0\sim k_1$, contradicting with the independency of $H_0\cup K_1$.

label: S-S-Inverse
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{S-S-Inverse}
Let $H$ and $K$ be subgroups of $G$. We define the subset $\mathcal{S}$ as follows:
$$\mathcal{S}=\{S\subseteq G~|~ S\cap KH=\emptyset,~  S^{-1}K=S^{-1}*K,~ SH=S*H\}.$$ 
Note that $\emptyset \in \mathcal{S}$, and so $\mathcal{S}$ is  nonempty.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
Consider the dihedral group
$D_{12}=\langle a,b\mid a^6=b^2=1, ab=ba^{-1}\rangle$
and let $H=\langle b\rangle$ and $K=\langle a^3b\rangle$ be subgroups of $D_{12}$. Set $S=\{a,a^2,a^4,a^5\}$.
It is readily verified that $S\in\mathcal{S}$. Set $R=\{a^3b\}$ and $L=\{a^3\}$. Since \eqref{Construction} holds for $\mathrm{BC}(D_{12};R,L,S)$, it follows that $H_0\cup K_1$ is a subgroup perfect code in $D_{12}$.
head: environment

label: Property
title: Property
head: environment

label: Perfect-Property
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $S\in \mathcal{S}$ and $C=H_0\cup K_1$ be a subgroup perfect code in a bi-Cayley graph of $G$ such as $\Gamma=\mathrm{BC}(G;R,L,S)$. Suppose that $g_i\in G_0\cup G_1\setminus (S^{-1}*K)_0 \cup(S*H)_1$ with $(g^2)_i\in C$.  We continue the proof in the following two cases.
\begin{itemize}
  \item [(i)] We have $(g^2)_i\in H_0$.  From Lemma \ref{LeftTransversal}, $R\cup \{1_G\}$ is a left transversal of $H$ in $G\setminus S^{-1}*K$. So, there exists a unique $r\in R\cup \{1_G\}$ such that $g\in rH$. Therefore,  $gH=rH$ and since $H$ is normal in $G$, we have
       $$g^{-1}H=Hg^{-1}=Hr^{-1}=r^{-1}H.$$
       On the other hand, $g^2\in H$. Hence, we have $gH=g^{-1}H$ and $rH=r^{-1}H$. Since $r, r^{-1}\in R=R^{-1}$ and $R$ is a left transversal of $H$ in $G\setminus S^{-1}*H$, we conclude that $r=r^{-1}$ and $r^2=1_G$. This together with $g\in rH$ imply that there is some $h\in H$ for which we have $(gh)^2=1_G$.
  \item [(ii)] If $(g^2)_i\in K_1$. Then, $g^2\in K$ and $g\in G\setminus S*H$.  From Lemma \ref{LeftTransversal}, $L\cup \{1_G\}$ is a left transversal of $K$ in $G\setminus S*H$. So, there exists a unique $l\in L\cup \{1_G\}$ such that $g\in lK$. Therefore,  $gK=lK$ and since $K$ is normal in $G$, we have
       $$g^{-1}K=Kg^{-1}=Kl^{-1}=l^{-1}K.$$
        As $g^2\in K$, we have $gK=g^{-1}K$ and $lK=l^{-1}K$. Since $l, l^{-1}\in L=L^{-1}$ and $L\cup \{1_G\}$ is a left transversal of $K$ in $G\setminus S*H$, we conclude that $l=l^{-1}$ and $l^2=1_G$. This together with $g\in lK$ imply that there is some $k\in K$ for which we have $(gk)^2=1_G$.
\end{itemize} 
To prove the sufficiency, suppose that $H$ and $K$ are normal subgroups of $G$  and $S\in \mathcal{S}$ and Property \eqref{Property} holds. We now construct inverse-closed subsets $R,L \subseteq G$ such that \eqref{Construction} holds. 
\begin{itemize}
  \item 
  We consider two following sets:
  \begin{align*}
    I_1= & \{x_1H,\dots, x_rH~|~\forall~1\leqslant i\leqslant r:~  x_iH\notin S^{-1}*K, ~ x_iH=(x_iH)^{-1}\}, \\
    I_2= & \{y_1H,\dots, y_sH~|~\forall~1\leqslant i\leqslant s:~y_iH\notin S^{-1}*K, ~ y_iH\neq(y_iH)^{-1}\}.
  \end{align*}
    For each $x_iH\in I_1$, where $1\leq i\leq r$, pick an element $x_ih \in x_iH$. 
     We have $(x_ih)_0\in G_0\setminus (S^{-1}*K)_0$ and $(x_i^2)_0\in H_0$.
     Since $x_i^2\in H$, there exists an element $h^{\prime}\in H$ such that $x_i=x_i^{-1}h^{\prime}$ and so, $(x_ih)^2=x_ihx_i^{-1}h^{\prime}h\in H$ because $H$ is normal in $G$.
      So according to property \ref{Property}, there exists $h_i\in H$ such that $(x_ihh_i)^2=1_G$. Set $z_i:=x_ihh_i$. Note that $z_i H=x_iH\notin S^{-1}*K$. Finally, we construct the inverse-closed set $R$ as follows:
    $$R=\{z_1, \dots, z_r,y_1, y_1^{-1},\dots, y_s, y_s^{-1}\}$$ 
    which is a left transversal of $H$ in $G\setminus S^{-1}*K$.
 \item 
 We define two sets as follows:
  \begin{align*}
    I_1= & \{x_1K,\dots, x_rK~|~\forall~1\leqslant i\leqslant r:~  x_iK\notin  S*H, ~ x_iK=(x_iK)^{-1}\}, \\
    I_2= & \{y_1K,\dots, y_sK~|~\forall~1\leqslant i\leqslant s:~y_iK\notin S*H, ~ y_iK\neq(y_iK)^{-1}\}.
  \end{align*}
    For each $x_iK\in I_1$, pick an element $x_ik \in x_iK$. 
     We have $(x_ik)_0\in G_0\setminus (S*H)_0$ and $(x^2_i)_0\in K_0$.
     Since $x_i^2\in K$, there exists an element $k^{\prime}\in K$ such that $x_i=x_i^{-1}k^{\prime}$ and so, $(x_ik)^2=x_ikx_i^{-1}k^{\prime}k\in K$ because $K$ is normal in $G$.
      So according to property \ref{Property}, there exists $k_i\in K$ such that $(x_ikk_i)^2=1_G$. Set $z_i:=x_ikk_i$. Note that $z_i K=x_iK\notin S*H$.  Finally, we construct the inverse-closed set $L$ as follows:
    $$L=\{z_1, \dots, z_r,y_1, y_1^{-1},\dots, y_s, y_s^{-1}\}.$$ 
 \end{itemize} 
Hence, $H_0\cup K_1$ is a perfect code in $\mathrm{BC}(G, R, L, S)$ and the proof is completed.

label: OddOrder
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{OddOrder}
  Let $H$ and $K$ be normal subgroups of $G$. If either $|H|$ or $|G/H|$ and $|K|$ or $|G/K|$ is odd, then $H_0\cup K_1$ is a subgroup perfect code of $G$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We let $S\in \mathcal{S}$ and $C=H_0\cup K_1$. We prove that Property \ref{Property} holds. Suppose that  $g_i\in G_0\cup G_1\setminus (S^{-1}*K)_0 \cup(S*H)_1$ with $(g^2)_i\in C$. Therefore, $g^2\in H$ or $g^2\in K$. Suppose that $g^2\in H$. We continue the proof in the following two cases.
\begin{itemize}
  \item Assume that $|H|$ is odd. Then, $(g^2)^{2k+1}=1_G$ for some integer $k$. Define $h:=g^{2k}$. since  $g^{2k}=(g^2)^k$, it follows that 
      $h\in H$. Moreover,
      $$(gh)^2=g^{4k+2}=(g^2)^{2k+1}=1_G.$$
  \item Let $|G/H|$ be odd. Since $g^2\in H$, it follows that $(gH)^2=H$. Therefore, $gH=H$ because $o(gH)\leqslant 2$ and $o(gH)$ divides $|G/H|$ which is an odd number. Consequently, $g\in H$. Set $h:=g^{-1}\in H$. Evidently, we have $(gh)^2=1_G$.
\end{itemize}
 In the case that $g^2\in K$,  by a similar argument to when $g^2\in H$, we conclude that there exists some $k\in K$ such that $(gk)^2=1_G$.  Therefore, Property \ref{Property} holds and $C$ is a perfect code of $G$.
head: environment

label: AbeliSEmpty
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{AbeliSEmpty}
 Let $G$ be an abelian group and $H$ be a non-trivial subgroup of $G$.  If $\{e_0\}\cup H_1$ is a perfect code in a bi-Cayley graph $\mathrm{BC}(G;R, L, S)$, then $S=\emptyset$.
head: environment

label: ss-1
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $C=\{e_0\}\cup H_1$ be a perfect code in a bi-Cayley graph $\mathrm{BC}(G;R, L, S)$. Suppose, to the contrary, that $S\neq \emptyset$.  We firstly prove that $S=S^{-1}$. By \eqref{Construction},  we obtain
   $$G=L*H\mathbin{\dot\cup} S\mathbin{\dot\cup} H.$$
   Since $G$ is abeli and $L$ is inverse-closed, $G^{-1}=G=L*H\mathbin{\dot\cup} S^{-1}\mathbin{\dot\cup} H$ and hence, $S=S^{-1}$. Since $S\neq \emptyset$, we let $s, s^{-1}\in S$. We obtain 
   \begin{equation}\label{ss-1}
    s_0\sim e_1~~\text{and}~~s_1\sim e_0.
   \end{equation}
   Take $e\neq h\in H $. Note that $hs\notin H$ because otherwise we would have $S\cap H\neq \emptyset$ which contradicts Claim \ref{SInterKH}. Therefore, $(hs)_1$ is outside $C$ and must have a neighbor in $C$. If $(hs)_1\sim e_0$, then we have $s^{\prime}hs=e$ and $s^{\prime}s=h^{-1}$, for some $s^{\prime}\in S$. Consequently, we obtain $s_0\sim (h^{-1})_1$, a contradiction with \eqref{ss-1}. If $(hs)_1\sim h^{\prime}_1$ for $h^{\prime}\in H$, then $lhs=h^{\prime}$ and $ls=h^{\prime}h^{-1}$. So, $s_1\sim (h^{\prime}h^{-1})_1$, contradicting \eqref{ss-1}. Therefore, $(hs)_1$ has no neighbor in $C$.

title: Corollary
body_md: Let $G$ be of odd cardinality. Then, for normal subgroups $H$ and $K$ of $G$, $H_0\cup K_1$ is a subgroup perfect code.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Since $|H|$ and $|K|$ are divisors of $|G|$, $|H|$ and $|K|$ must be odd. So, it follows from Corollary \ref{OddOrder} that $H_0 \cup K_1$ is a subgroup perfect code of $G$.

label: P-Sylow-Intersection
title: Claim
body_md:
\label{P-Sylow-Intersection}
 Let $G$ be an abelian group and $P$ be a Sylow 2-subgroup of $G$. Then, every subgroup $H$ of $G$ can be written as 
$$H=(H\cap P)\times (H\cap Q),$$
where $Q$ is the Hall $2^{\prime}$-subgroup of $G$.
head: environment

title: Claim
body_md:
Suppose that $H$ is a subgroup of $G$ and $S$ is a subset of $G$. If $P$ is a Sylow $2$-subgroup of $G$, then we have 
   $$P \cap (S*H) \subseteq (S\cap P)*(H\cap P).$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We know that $G=P\times Q$, where $Q$ is the Hall $2^{\prime}$-subgroup of $G$. Let $x\in P\cap (S*H)$. Then, $x=sh$, for some $s\in S$ and $h\in H$. Moreover, $s= s_ps_q$ and $h=h_ph_q$ with $s_p,h_p\in P$ and $s_q,h_q\in Q$.
 Since $x\in P$, we must have $s_qh_q=1$. On the other hand, $s_p\in S\cap P$ and $h_p\in H\cap P$. Therefore, $x=s_ph_p\in (S\cap P)*(H\cap P)$.
head: environment

label: SylowLem
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{SylowLem}
  Let $H$ and $K$ be subgroups of $G$ and  $P$ be a Sylow 2-subgroup of $G$. If $H_0 \cup K_1$  is a subgroup perfect code of $G$, then $(H\cap P)_0\cup (K\cap P)_1 $ is a subgroup perfect code of $P$.
head: environment

label: Sylow
title: Proof
body_md:
We know that $G=P\times Q$, where $Q$ is the Hall $2^{\prime}$-subgroup of $G$. 
  Suppose that $H_0\cup K_1$ is a subgroup perfect code of $G$. Set
   $S\in \mathcal{S}$,
  $S_p=S\cap P$, $H_p=H\cap P$, $K_p=K\cap P$, and $C_p=(H_p)_0 \cup (K_p)_1$. We want to prove that the following statement holds:
  \begin{equation}\label{Sylow}
    \forall g_i\in (P_0\cup P_1)\setminus ((S_p^{-1}*K_p)_0 \cup(S_p*K_p)_1),  ~ (g^2)_i\in C_p~\Rightarrow~\exists x_i\in C_p:~ ~(gx)^2=1_G.
  \end{equation} 
   Assume that $g_i\in P_0\cup P_1\setminus (S_p^{-1}*K_p)_0 \cup(S_p*H_p)_1$ with $(g^2)_i\in C_p$. Note that $g_i\notin (S^{-1}*K)_0 \cup(S*H)_1$ because otherwise $g\in P\cap  S^{-1}*K$ or $g\in P\cap S*H$. This together with Claim \ref{P-Sylow-Intersection} imply that $g\in S_p^{-1}*K_p$ or $g\in S_p*H_p$ which contradicts the assumption in \eqref{Sylow}. Therefore, by Property \ref{Property}, there exists some $x_i\in C$ such that $(gx)^2=1_G$. We note that  $x^{-2}=g^{-2}\in H_p$ when $i=0$, and $x^{-2}\in K_p$ if $i=1$, and so, $x\in H_p$ when $i=0$, and $x\in K_p$ if $i=1$, which implies that $x_i\in C_p$.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
Let $G=\langle a \rangle \times \langle b \rangle \times  \langle c \rangle$, where $o(a)=4$, $o(b)=3$, and $o(c)=5$. The Sylow 2-subgroup of $G$ is $P=\langle a \rangle$. Let $H=\langle b \rangle$, $K=\langle c \rangle$.  Suppose that 
     $$\Gamma =\mathrm{BC}(P;\{a, a^3\},\{a, a^3\},\{a^2\}),$$
      as shown in Figure \ref{SylowFig}. Then  
      $(H\cap P)_0\cup (K\cap P)_1=\{e_0, e_1\}$
       is a perfect code of $\Gamma$. 
       However, $C=H_0\cup K_1$ cannot be a perfect code in any connected bi-Cayley graph over $G$. Indeed, suppose that there exists a bi-Cayley graph $\mathrm{BC}(G; R, L, S)$ that admits $C$ as a perfect code. By 
     \eqref{Construction}, we must have 
     $$60=3|R|+3+5|S|~~  \text{and}~~ 60=5|L|+5+3|S|.$$ The first equation implies that $|S|\in \{0, 3, 6, 9\}$, whereas the second implies that $|S|\in \{0,5,10,15\}$. Thus, the only possible common value is $|S|=0$. Since $S=\emptyset$ implies that the bi-Cayley graph is disconnected, no connected bi-Cayley graph over $G$ can admit $C$ as a perfect code.

label: EquSyl
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{EquSyl}
  Let $H$ and $K$ be subgroups of $G$ such that $ H\leq K$ and  $P$ be a Sylow 2-subgroup of $G$. Then,  $H_0 \cup K_1$  is a subgroup perfect code of $G$ if and only if $(H\cap P)_0\cup (K\cap P)_1 $ is a subgroup perfect code of $P$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The necessity follows from Lemma \ref{SylowLem}.

    For the sufficiency, suppose that $G=P\times Q$, where $Q$ is the $2^{\prime}$-Hall subgroup of $G$. Set $H_p:=H\cap P$, $H_q:=H\cap Q$, $K_p:=K\cap P$, and $K_q:=K\cap Q$. Let \eqref{Sylow} holds. We find a bi-Cayley graph in which $H_0 \cup K_1$ is a perfect code.
    Let $S\in \mathcal{S}$ and $S$ be inverse-closed.
      Let $g_i\in G_0\cup G_1\setminus (S^{-1}*K)_0 \cup(S*H)_1$ with $(g^2)_i\in H_0\cup K_1$.
  We write $g=g_pg_q$, where $g_p\in P$ and $g_q\in Q$.
  With Claim \ref{P-Sylow-Intersection}, since  $g^2=g_p^2g_q^2\in H\cup K$, it follows that $g_p^2\in H_p\cup K_p$ and $g_q^2\in H_q\cup K_q$. On the other hand, $g_q$ has odd order because $o(g_q)$ divides $|H_q\cup K_q|$, which is odd.  This implies that
  \begin{equation}\label{gq}
    g_q=g_q^2 g_q^{2k}\in H_q\cup K_q.
  \end{equation} 
  We now note that $(g_p)_i\notin(S_p^{-1}*K_p)_0 \cup (S_p*H_p)_1$ because otherwise if  $g_p\in  S_p^{-1}*K_p$, then $g_p=s^{-1}_pk_p$, where $s_p\in S_p$ and $k_p\in K_p$. Using \eqref{gq}, $g=g_pg_q= s^{-1}_pk_p g_q\in S^{-1}*K$ which is a contradiction. Similarly, if we consider $g_p\in  S_p*H_p$, then $g_p=s_ph_p$, where $s_p\in S_p$ and $h_p\in h_p$. This leads to $g=g_pg_q= s_ph_p g_q\in S*K=S^{-1}*K$ by \eqref{gq}, a contradiction.
          We now conclude from \eqref{Sylow} that there exists $(x_p)_i\in (H_p)_0\cup (K_p)_1$  satisfying $(g_px_p)^2=1_G$.
  We now let $x:= x_pg_q^{-1}$ which is an element of $H\cup K$. We have $(gx)^2=(g_pg_qx_pg_q^{-1})^2=1_G$ and so, $H_0\cup K_1$ is a subgroup perfect code of $G$.

title: Proposition
body_md: Let $G$ be an abelian group and $H$ and $K$ be subgroups of $G$ such that $H\leq K$. If $H_0 \cup K_1$ is a perfect code of a bi-Cayley graph $\mathrm{BC}(G;R, L, S)$, where $S$ is nontrivial and $S=S^{-1}$, then $H=K$.

label: ProjectEx
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ProjectEx}
  Let $G=\langle a\rangle \times \langle b\rangle$, where both $a$ and $b$ have order 4. Then the Sylow 2-subgroup of $G$ is $P=G$. Let $H=\langle a^{2}\rangle$, and define
$$R=L=\{b^{2}\}, \qquad
S=\{a,ab,ab^{2},ab^{3},b,b^{3}\}.$$
It is straightforward to verify that both $R\cup S^{-1}\cup{1_G}$ and $L\cup S\cup{1_G}$ are left transversals of $H$ in $G$. Hence, by Corollary~\ref{LeftTransversal}, $H$ is a subgroup perfect code of $\mathrm{BC}(G;R,L,S)$. On the other hand,
$
H\cap P=\langle a^{2}\rangle
$
which projects onto neither $\langle a\rangle$ nor $\langle b\rangle$.

label: OneCyclic
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{OneCyclic}
  Let $G$ be an abelian group, and let $H,K\leq G$. Suppose that
$P=\langle a_1\rangle\times\cdots\times\langle a_n\rangle$
is a Sylow $2$-subgroup of $G$, where $o(a_i)=2^{m_i}$ for $1\leq i\leq n$. If $H_0\cup K_1$ is a subgroup perfect code of $\mathrm{BC}(G;R,L,\emptyset)$, then each of $H\cap P$ and $K\cap P$ is either trivial or projects onto at least one of the $\langle a_i\rangle$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\Gamma=\mathrm{BC}(G;R,L,\emptyset)$, and suppose that $H_0\cup K_1$ is a subgroup perfect code in $\Gamma$. Since $S=\emptyset$, we can view $\Gamma$ as the disjoint union of two Cayley graphs,
$\Gamma_0=\mathrm{Cay}(G_0,R)$ and $\Gamma_1=\mathrm{Cay}(G_1,L)$.
Since $H_0$ is a subgroup perfect code in $\Gamma_0$, \cite[Lemma 2.6]{Huang-2018} implies that $H\cap P$ is either trivial or projects onto at least one direct factor $\langle a_i\rangle$. Similarly, since $K_1$ is a subgroup perfect code in $\Gamma_1$, \cite[Lemma 2.6]{Huang-2018} implies that $K\cap P$ is either trivial or projects onto at least one direct factor $\langle a_i\rangle$.
head: environment

label: ExOneCyclic
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ExOneCyclic}
 Let $G=\langle a \rangle \times \langle b \rangle$, where both $a$ and $b$ have order 4. Set 
 $H=\langle a, b^2 \rangle$.
Then, $\pi _1(H)=\langle a \rangle$. Take $g_0=b_0\in G_0$. Then, $(g^2)_0=(b^2)_0\in H_0$. On the other hand, every element $h\in H$ has the form $h=a^ib^{2j}$, where $i\in \{0, 1,2,3\}$ and $j\in \{0,1\}$. Hence,  
$gh=a^ib^{2j+1}$,
 and therefore 
 $(gh)^2=a^{2i}b^2\neq 1_G$. Therefore, by Theorem~\ref{Perfect-Property}, $H$ cannot be a perfect code in any bi-Cayley graph.
head: environment

label: ThCyclic
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The necessity holds by Lemma \ref{OneCyclic}.

To prove the sufficiency, let $\Gamma=\mathrm{BC}(G;R,L,\emptyset)$. Since $S=\emptyset$, $\Gamma$ is a disjoint union of two Cayley graphs
$\Gamma_0=\mathrm{Cay}(G_0,R)$ and $\Gamma_1=\mathrm{Cay}(G_1,L)$.
By \cite[Theorem 2.7]{Huang-2018}, $H_0$ is a  perfect code of $\Gamma_0$ and $K_1$ is a  perfect code of $\Gamma_1$. Therefore, $H_0\cup K_1$ is a  perfect code of $\Gamma$.

title: Corollary
body_md: Suppose that $G$ is a cyclic group and $H, K\leq G$. Then, $H_0 \cup K_1$ is a subgroup perfect code of some bi-Cayley graph $\mathrm{BC}(G; R,L, \emptyset)$ if and only if either $|H|$ or $|G/H|$ is odd, and either $|K|$ or $|G/K|$ is odd.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: By Theorem \ref{ThCyclic}, $H$ is a subgroup perfect code of $G$ if and only if $H\cap P$ is either trivial or equal to $P$, where $P$ is the Sylow 2-subgroup of $G$.  Moreover, $H\cap P$ is trivial if and only if $|H|$ is odd, while $H\cap P=P$ if and only if $|G/H|$ is odd. The same statements hold for $K$.

Let $H=\{1,b\}$ and $K=\{e\}$ be two subgroups of $D_{2n}$. Then, $H_0\cup K_1$ is a subgroup perfect code of $D_{2n}$.

title: Proposition
body_md: Let $H=\{1,b\}$ and $K=\{1, a^{n/2}b\}$ be two subgroups of $D_{2n}$, where $n$ is an even number. Then, $H_0\cup K_1$ is a subgroup perfect code of $D_{2n}$.

title: Proof
body_md: We let $S=\langle a \rangle \setminus\{1, a^{n/2}\}$, $R=\{a^{n/2}b\}$, and $L=\{a^{n/2}\}$.  It is easy to verify that \eqref{Construction} holds.
